sections.body:
AI-Based Early Warning and Landslide Risk Monitoring System in NER


Problem Statement ID

Problem Statement Title


AI-Based Early Warning and Landslide Risk Monitoring System in NER


1. Introduction


The North Eastern Region (NER) frequently faces landslides, flash floods, road blockages, and slope failures due to heavy rainfall, fragile terrain, and unplanned hill cutting. These incidents often disrupt connectivity, damage infrastructure, delay emergency response, and isolate remote villages for days.


Currently, monitoring of vulnerable zones is mostly reactive and dependent on manual reporting. There is limited use of real-time predictive systems for identifying high-risk zones and issuing early warnings to authorities and local communities. With increasing climate vulnerability in the region, there is a need for an AI-enabled real-time monitoring and prediction system that can help authorities take preventive action before disasters occur.


2. Problem Statement


The proposed system aims to develop an AI-powered early warning and monitoring platform capable of predicting and tracking landslide-prone areas in real time across the North Eastern Region.


The solution should:


Collect and analyse rainfall patterns.


Use satellite imagery for monitoring terrain and environmental changes.


Use terrain and slope data to identify vulnerable areas.


Use historical landslide records for AI/ML-based learning.


Identify high-risk zones and predict possible landslide events.


Provide real-time alerts to district administrations, disaster management authorities, and local communities.


Integrate GIS mapping for visualization of vulnerable roads, villages, and infrastructure.


Allow citizens and field officials to upload geo-tagged photos/videos of cracks, slope movement, or blocked roads.


Generate dashboards for risk severity, road connectivity, weather-linked forecasts, and emergency response prioritisation.


Support multilingual notifications and low-network/offline functionality for remote areas.


3. Objectives


Develop a centralized AI-enabled platform for landslide risk monitoring.


Predict landslide risk using rainfall, soil moisture, satellite, terrain, and historical data.


Identify and visualize high-risk zones using GIS-based maps and risk heatmaps.


Provide early warnings to authorities and communities before potential landslide events.


Monitor vulnerable roads, villages, and critical infrastructure.


Enable field officials and citizens to submit geo-tagged evidence.


Support emergency response prioritisation using risk severity and connectivity information.


Provide multilingual alerts suitable for communities in the North Eastern Region.


Support offline data collection and synchronization in low-network areas.


Build a scalable cloud-based architecture that can integrate multiple real-time data sources.


4. Proposed Solution


The system is a scalable AI-based software platform consisting of a web dashboard, mobile/field application, GIS visualization layer, data ingestion services, and an AI/ML prediction engine.


4.1 Working Process


Collect rainfall, soil moisture, satellite imagery, terrain/slope, and historical landslide data.


Receive real-time or periodic updates from connected APIs, satellite feeds, and sensors.


Pre-process and standardize the collected data.


Combine multiple data sources to create a risk profile for each monitored area.


Run AI/ML models to estimate landslide risk and identify high-risk zones.


Display risk levels and vulnerable locations on a GIS map.


Monitor roads, villages, and infrastructure located inside or near high-risk zones.


Allow citizens and field officials to upload geo-tagged photos/videos and field observations.


Generate alerts when risk crosses configured thresholds.


Prioritize emergency response based on severity, affected connectivity, population/infrastructure exposure, and field reports.


Store data in the cloud and synchronize offline field reports when network connectivity becomes available.


5. System Architecture


5.1 Frontend


Web dashboard for administrators and disaster management authorities.


Mobile/field interface for officials and citizens.


GIS map-based visualization.


Risk heatmaps and location-based alerts.


Incident reporting and status tracking.


Multilingual notification interface.


5.2 Backend


Handles business logic and data processing.


Collects data from APIs, satellite feeds, and sensors.


Runs AI/ML prediction services.


Calculates risk scores and severity levels.


Processes geo-tagged reports.


Manages alerts and notification rules.


Handles offline synchronization and cloud data updates.


5.3 Database


User and official accounts.


Rainfall observations.


Soil moisture readings.


Satellite/remote-sensing observations.


Terrain and slope information.


Historical landslide records.


Geo-tagged photos/videos and field reports.


Road, village, and infrastructure information.


Risk scores, alerts, and response records.


5.4 AI/ML Prediction Engine


Combines environmental and historical features.


Identifies patterns associated with landslide occurrence.


Produces risk probability or risk category for monitored locations.


Supports continuous updating as new rainfall, sensor, satellite, or field data arrives.


Provides inputs for early warning and emergency prioritisation.


6. Key Features


6.1 Real-Time GIS Dashboard


Displays monitored locations on an interactive map.


Shows landslide risk heatmaps.


Highlights vulnerable roads, villages, and infrastructure.


Displays current alerts and affected areas.


Allows authorities to identify high-risk zones quickly.


6.2 AI/ML-Based Risk Prediction


Uses rainfall patterns.


Uses satellite imagery.


Uses terrain and slope characteristics.


Uses historical landslide records.


Produces location-wise risk levels.


Updates predictions as new data becomes available.


6.3 Risk Severity Levels


Low Risk – normal monitoring.


Moderate Risk – increased observation and preparedness.


High Risk – issue warning and prepare emergency response.


Critical Risk – immediate warning and response prioritisation.


6.4 Early Warning and Alerts


Automated alerts based on predicted risk.


Alerts for district administrations and disaster management authorities.


Community notifications through supported channels.


SMS/app-based warning mechanism.


Multilingual notifications.


Escalation for critical risk conditions.


6.5 Sensor Integration


Live readings can supplement rainfall, terrain, satellite, and historical data.


6.6 Satellite and Terrain Integration


Satellite feeds can support large-area monitoring.


Satellite imagery can help identify environmental and terrain changes.


Digital terrain/slope information can help identify naturally vulnerable areas.


These data sources can be combined with rainfall and soil moisture information.


6.7 Geo-Tagged Citizen and Field Reporting


Upload photos/videos from affected locations.


Automatically associate reports with geographic coordinates.


Report cracks, slope movement, blocked roads, or other visible warning signs.


Allow authorities to verify and use field observations for response.


6.8 Road Connectivity Monitoring


Display vulnerable and affected roads on the GIS map.


Record road blockage reports.


Show connectivity status.


Support emergency route prioritisation.


Help authorities identify isolated villages and critical routes.


6.9 Emergency Response Prioritisation


Prioritize areas with critical landslide risk.


Consider affected roads and connectivity.


Consider vulnerable villages and infrastructure.


Combine model predictions with field reports.


Help authorities allocate response resources efficiently.


6.10 Offline and Low-Network Support


Allow field officials to collect data when connectivity is poor.


Store reports locally on the device.


Synchronize stored reports when connectivity returns.


Reduce dependence on continuous internet connectivity in remote areas.


7. Data Sources


Rainfall patterns and weather observations.


Satellite imagery and satellite-derived observations.


Terrain and slope/elevation data.


Historical landslide records.


Road and infrastructure geographic data.


Citizen and field-official geo-tagged reports.


8. AI/ML Prediction Approach


The prediction engine can treat each monitored geographic area as a location whose landslide risk changes over time. Environmental, terrain, historical, and field-report features are combined to estimate the current risk level.


8.1 Input Features


Recent and cumulative rainfall.


Rainfall intensity and patterns.


Soil moisture level.


Slope and terrain characteristics.


Historical landslide occurrence.


Satellite-derived changes where available.


Recent citizen/field observations.


Road and infrastructure exposure.


8.2 Prediction Output


Location-wise landslide risk score.


Risk category: Low, Moderate, High, or Critical.


Potentially affected zones.


Warning/alert recommendation.


Inputs for emergency response prioritisation.


9. Risk Scoring Concept


A practical prototype can combine normalized environmental and exposure indicators into a risk score. The exact weights should be calibrated using historical data and validated against known landslide events.


Example conceptual structure:


Risk Score = W₁×Rainfall + W₂×Soil Moisture + W₃×Slope/Terrain + W₄×Historical Risk + W₅×Satellite/Field Indicators


10. Workflow


User/official opens the application or dashboard.


System receives available weather, rainfall, sensor, satellite, and terrain data.


Data is cleaned and converted into model-ready features.


AI/ML engine calculates risk for monitored locations.


GIS dashboard displays the risk heatmap.


High-risk areas are identified automatically.


System checks affected roads, villages, and infrastructure.


Citizens/officials can submit geo-tagged photos/videos.


New observations are incorporated into monitoring and decision support.


Alerts are generated for relevant authorities and communities.


Emergency response is prioritized.


Offline reports synchronize with the cloud once connectivity is restored.


11. Dashboard


11.1 Authority Dashboard


Overall regional risk map.


District-wise risk summary.


High-risk and critical locations.


Rainfall-linked risk forecast.


Road connectivity status.


Affected villages and infrastructure.


Citizen/field reports.


Active alerts.


Emergency response prioritisation.


11.2 Field/Mobile Dashboard


Current location and nearby risk.


Risk warning notifications.


Submit photo/video reports.


Report road blockage or slope movement.


View assigned incidents.


Offline data collection.


Sync pending reports.


12. Alert Levels and Suggested Actions


Risk Level


Meaning


Suggested Action


Low


No immediate indication of significant risk.


Routine monitoring.


Moderate


Environmental conditions require closer observation.


Increase monitoring and preparedness.


High


Conditions indicate elevated landslide possibility.


Issue warning and prepare response teams.


Critical


Very high-risk conditions or strong warning signals.


Immediate alert and emergency response prioritisation.


13. Technologies / Components


Web frontend for authority and administrative dashboards.


Mobile application for field reporting and alerts.


Backend APIs for data ingestion and application logic.


GIS mapping platform for spatial visualization.


Cloud database and storage.


AI/ML service for risk prediction.


Weather/meteorological API integration.


Satellite data/feed integration.


SMS and app notification services.


Offline local storage and synchronization mechanism.


14. Advantages


Moves disaster management from reactive reporting toward predictive risk monitoring.


Provides a single view of risk across multiple data sources.


Supports real-time GIS visualization.


Enables early warnings before potential disaster events.


Improves prioritisation of emergency resources.


Supports monitoring of remote and vulnerable areas.


Combines AI predictions with field observations.


Improves visibility of road and village connectivity.


Supports multilingual communication.


Offline sync improves usability in low-network regions.


Scalable for deployment across the North Eastern Region.


15. Limitations


Prediction quality depends on the availability and quality of training data.


Real-time monitoring may depend on external API and satellite data availability.


AI predictions are probabilistic and cannot guarantee that a landslide will occur.


Cloud synchronization may be delayed in areas with very weak connectivity.


Satellite observations may not always provide the required frequency or resolution.


Field reports and uploaded media may require verification.


16. Future Scope


More advanced deep-learning models for satellite imagery.


Automated detection of cracks and slope changes from images/videos.


Integration with additional government disaster-management systems.


More detailed population and infrastructure exposure modelling.


Automated route recommendations for emergency teams.


Improved multilingual voice-based alerts.


Long-term climate and landslide susceptibility forecasting.


Digital twin or 3D terrain visualization for selected high-risk locations.


17. Citizen Evidence Intelligence, Trust & Action Engine


The platform shall treat citizen and field reports as an important real-time evidence layer. Users/citizens can upload a photo or video of a suspected landslide, crack, slope movement, fallen debris, water seepage, or blocked road. The system automatically captures the report location and performs AI-assisted analysis before routing the report for appropriate action.


17.1 Citizen Photo/Video Upload


Citizens can upload photos and/or videos directly from the mobile or web application.


The application requests location permission and automatically captures GPS coordinates when available.


The system reverse-geocodes the coordinates to automatically display Area/Locality, City/Town, District, and State where available.


Every report stores latitude, longitude, timestamp, media, detected problem type, and automatically fetched location.


Users can manually correct the displayed location if GPS accuracy is poor, while retaining the original captured coordinates for audit purposes.


The user should not need to type the full address manually in normal operation.


17.2 AI Evidence Verification


AI analyses uploaded media to determine whether it contains visual evidence relevant to the reported problem.


AI produces an evidence assessment such as Genuine/Likely Genuine, Suspicious, or Insufficient Evidence.


AI checks for signs consistent with AI-generated or heavily manipulated media and can classify media as Likely Original, Potentially AI-Generated/Manipulated, or Unknown.


AI identifies the apparent problem category, such as landslide/debris, road blockage, crack, slope movement, or other visible hazard.


AI estimates the apparent severity/criticality of the visible problem and classifies it as Low, Moderate, High, or Critical.


AI results are decision-support signals rather than absolute proof; suspicious or high-impact cases can be routed for human verification.


17.3 Citizen Trust Score


Each registered citizen receives a dynamic trust score based on the reliability of their historical reports.


Verified and useful reports increase the citizen's trust score.


Repeated false, misleading, manipulated, or unverifiable reports reduce the trust score.


The score is recalculated as additional reports are reviewed and verified.


Trust score influences report confidence and prioritisation, but must not prevent a potentially life-threatening report from being reviewed.


Example Trust Score = (Verified Useful Reports ÷ Total Reviewed Reports) × 100


17.4 AI-Assisted Action Engine


Genuine + Critical → immediately raise a high-priority incident, notify the responsible authority, and place the location prominently on the GIS dashboard.


Genuine + High → create a priority field-verification/response task and issue an appropriate warning based on overall risk.


Genuine + Moderate/Low → store the observation, update local risk intelligence, and continue monitoring.


Suspicious or Potentially AI-Generated/Manipulated → mark the report for verification, reduce confidence in the evidence, and do not automatically treat the media as confirmed ground truth.


Insufficient Evidence → request additional photo/video or field verification where appropriate.


If citizen evidence coincides with independently elevated rainfall, sensor, satellite, terrain, or historical risk, the urgency of field verification can increase.


17.5 Automatic Location & Address Intelligence


Capture GPS latitude and longitude from the user's device.


Reverse-geocode coordinates to show Area/Locality, City/Town, District, State, and other available address components.


Display exact coordinates on the GIS map.


Show GPS accuracy where available.


Use location to identify nearby roads, villages, infrastructure, known landslide-prone zones, and administrative boundaries.


Attach geographic information to every report so authorities can locate the incident quickly.


17.6 Unified Risk + Citizen Evidence Score


The final operational priority should combine regional AI/ML landslide risk with citizen evidence quality and exposure. A conceptual model is:


Action Priority = W₁×Predicted Landslide Risk + W₂×Evidence Confidence + W₃×Criticality + W₄×Exposure/Connectivity + W₅×Citizen Trust


The weights should be configurable and calibrated using historical incidents and authority feedback. Citizen trust is one supporting signal and should never override independent disaster indicators.


17.7 Interactive Citizen Experience


One-tap Report Hazard action from the home screen.


Camera/upload interface with clear guidance on what to photograph.


Automatic GPS, Area/City, and coordinates after permission is granted.


Live preview of detected issue type, AI evidence confidence, and apparent severity before submission.


Simple status flow: Submitted → AI Checked → Under Review → Action Assigned → Resolved.


Citizens can view their trust score, report history, and the action/status taken on their reports where disclosure is appropriate.


Multilingual and voice-assisted reporting can improve accessibility.


18. UI/UX, 3D Visualization & Professional Design


The platform should have a highly polished, professional, interactive interface suitable for government authorities, disaster-management teams, field officials, and citizens. The UI should prioritize clarity and rapid decision-making while using modern 3D and motion design where it improves understanding.


18.1 Authority Dashboard Design


Professional command-center layout with a large interactive GIS map as the primary workspace.


Animated risk heatmaps and 3D terrain visualization for selected vulnerable zones.


Real-time counters for Critical, High, Moderate, and Low-risk locations.


Animated alert cards for new critical incidents.


Interactive drill-down from Region → District → City/Area → Incident.


3D markers or elevated terrain indicators for high-risk slopes and important infrastructure.


Road connectivity overlays showing blocked, vulnerable, and operational routes.


Charts for rainfall, soil moisture, risk trends, reports, and response times.


Filters for time, district, risk level, incident type, data source, and verification status.


18.2 Citizen App Design


Clean, simple home screen with a prominent Report Hazard button.


Interactive map showing nearby risk and warnings.


Camera-first reporting flow with automatic location detection.


Visible AI verification status after upload.


Clear display of detected problem, apparent severity, evidence confidence, and report status.


Minimal typing through automatic address and location fetching.


Smooth micro-animations, transitions, cards, progress indicators, and interactive feedback.


Offline-first reporting screen showing Pending Sync when network is unavailable.


18.3 3D & Animation Principles


Use 3D terrain and elevation visualization to make slope risk easier to understand.


Use subtle animated terrain layers, map transitions, incident pulses, and risk-zone highlighting.


Use interactive 3D incident markers that open detailed evidence panels.


Use smooth camera transitions when moving from a district overview to a specific incident.


Use animated charts for live environmental trends.


Use professional motion design with restrained effects so critical warnings remain visually dominant.


Provide reduced-motion accessibility settings for users who prefer minimal animation.


18.4 Professional UI Requirements


Responsive design for desktop, tablet, and mobile.


Consistent typography, spacing, icons, cards, and component behavior.


Clear visual hierarchy for emergency information.


Accessible contrast and readable warning labels.


Dark/light interface options where appropriate.


Fast loading and optimized map/media rendering.


Loading skeletons and graceful error states for live data sources.


Clear data-source labels distinguishing AI prediction, sensor data, satellite data, and citizen reports.


Audit-friendly incident pages containing timestamp, coordinates, address, uploaded media, AI results, verification status, trust-score contribution, and actions taken.


18.5 End-to-End Citizen Report Example


A citizen sees a road partially blocked by a slope failure and taps Report Hazard. The application captures GPS coordinates and automatically fetches the Area/City/District address. The citizen uploads a photo. AI checks the image for relevance, apparent authenticity, possible AI-generation/manipulation, and visible severity. The system combines this evidence with current rainfall, soil moisture, terrain, historical risk, and nearby infrastructure information. If the combined evidence indicates a critical incident, the system raises the incident priority, places it prominently on the GIS dashboard, alerts the appropriate authority, and creates a response task. The citizen's trust score is updated after verification and subsequent authority feedback. The complete event is retained as an auditable record.


19. Conclusion


The AI-Based Early Warning and Landslide Risk Monitoring System in NER provides a scalable approach for improving landslide preparedness and disaster response. By combining rainfall, soil moisture, satellite imagery, terrain/slope information, historical landslide records, GIS, AI/ML prediction, and geo-tagged field reporting, the platform can identify high-risk areas and support timely warnings.


The integration of real-time dashboards, road and infrastructure monitoring, multilingual alerts, and offline synchronization makes the solution suitable for remote and connectivity-constrained areas of the North Eastern Region. The system is intended to support authorities and communities in taking preventive action, reducing potential loss of life and infrastructure, and strengthening climate-resilient governance.
